content: 1. Basic Training for Primary and Community-Level Providers: Healthcare providers working at the primary and community levels should receive 20–40 hours of basic training to equip them with foundational palliative care skills. 2. Intermediate Training for Secondary and Tertiary-Level Providers: Physicians and nurses managing cancer patients at secondary and tertiary care levels should undergo 60–80 hours of intermediate-level training to enhance their ability to provide specialized care. 3. Specialized Training for Palliative Care Teams: Specialized teams or palliative care units at secondary and tertiary levels should receive advanced training lasting 3–6 months to develop proficiency in delivering comprehensive palliative care. 4. Undergraduate Training in Medical and Nursing Schools: The African Palliative Care Association has developed a core palliative care curriculum and a framework of core competencies, which have been adopted by some African countries. Similarly, the European Association for Palliative Care (EAPC) has created a set of core competencies for palliative care professionals. Numerous free online training courses and resources are also available to support education in this field. In Latin America, a project titled Transforming the System was initiated to promote the teaching of palliative care in medical and nursing schools and integrate it into undergraduate curricula. This project was piloted in Colombia (2014–2015) and involved several steps: Initial visits to six universities to assess perceptions and interest in palliative care among faculty and students, which were met with positive responses. A workshop to identify palliative care competencies for undergraduate physicians and nurses, involving participants from 17 medical and nursing schools in Colombia. The agreed-upon competencies were translated into English and Spanish and made available on the International Association for Hospice and Palliative Care (IAHPC) website. Universities began using these competencies as a model to develop their own palliative care curricula tailored to their resources and students' needs. The project also planned a third phase to demonstrate innovative teaching methods for palliative care, with plans to expand to other Latin American countries, including Argentina in 2016. Public and Policy-Maker Education: The public should understand what palliative care entails, who should be referred, the services provided, and the benefits for patients and families. Policy-makers must recognize that palliative care is an integral part of the care continuum for diseases like cancer and HIV/AIDS, can be integrated into existing healthcare systems at a relatively low cost, and requires the availability of opioids at all levels of care. The media should disseminate reliable information about palliative care while respecting the dignity and rights of patients and families. Setting Standards and Evaluating Services: National palliative care standards should outline the requirements for establishing and operating palliative care services. Continuous quality improvement should be a priority for all palliative care providers, with data from quality indicators used to enhance services. Comparisons with similar services can help identify areas for improvement. Measuring Palliative Care Quality: Standardized clinical tools should be used to regularly assess symptom burden and functional ability. Costing and Funding Palliative Care: Palliative care has both direct and indirect costs, with personnel costs being the primary expense. Costing models, such as those developed in Romania and South Africa, calculate metrics like cost per inpatient day, cost per home visit, and cost per episode of care. Evidence shows that palliative care reduces overall healthcare costs by decreasing avoidable hospitalizations and unnecessary treatments while improving patients' quality of life. Case Examples: The African Palliative Care Association has developed standards for quality palliative care across Africa, focusing on home-based care and volunteer support. In South Africa, the Hospice Palliative Care Association has implemented an accreditation system with a star-rating framework to monitor and improve community-based palliative care services. These initiatives highlight the importance of integrating palliative care into healthcare systems, ensuring quality standards, and addressing cost-effectiveness to provide better care for patients with life-threatening illnesses.
